Article Title: Naga-Kuki clashes in Manipur: Kuki woman killed in Kamjong, severed head of Naga man found in Kangpokpi
Article Text:
Kuki-Zo woman, was killed in an ambush by suspected Naga militants, severed head of Naga man found

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is the most important step to reduce ethnic violence in Manipur? Dialogue between the communities Stronger security measures Greater efforts by the government Community-led peace initiatives 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion





GUWAHATI: A Kuki-Zo woman was killed and her husband injured in an alleged ambush by suspected Naga militants in Manipur’s Kamjong district on Thursday, while two other members of the community were reported missing as ethnic violence continued in the state.The deceased, Hatneikim Haokip, was from Molnoi village.Preliminary information suggests the group was travelling to Phaikoh to buy essential commodities when they were ambushed on the road between Phaikoh and Aishu. Hatneikim’s husband was injured, while the two other civilians who were with them remain missing.Thursday’s attack has taken the number of Kuki-Zo women killed in the Kuki-Naga clashes to 10, including two pregnant women. The clashes followed the Kuki-Meitei conflict that continued from 2023 to 2025.The attack came five days after nine people were killed across three districts, including two Kukis — one of them a woman — a Gorkha and six Naga men.Since the Kuki-Naga clashes began in Feb this year, at least 22 Naga and 32 Kuki-Zo people have been killed.Late on Wednesday night, security forces found the severed head of Naga man Ajinbou Ringkamai in Kangpokpi district.He was one of four Naga men killed when suspected Kuki militants attacked Makui Ashang village there on Oct 10. His head had been severed during the attack and remained missing. His headless body was taken to Jawaharlal Nehru Institute of Medical Sciences in Imphal on Oct 11.“The head was found in an isolated area near the site by security forces late on Wednesday night, and it was brought to JNIMS this morning for autopsy,” a senior official said.Joint Tribes Council Manipur, a Naga organisation, had given the authorities a 48-hour ultimatum to locate the head and ensure a proper funeral.Manipur home minister Govindas Konthoujam, speaking in Imphal on Thursday while visiting 84 BSF personnel admitted to Regional Institute of Medical Sciences with suspected food poisoning, said govt effort and security measures alone could not end the violence.“When the general people do not have humanity, then nobody can stop killing each other. We should understand that,” he said. “Killing will never solve any problem. We should talk to each other, and all differences should be resolved through dialogue.”He said govt was working to initiate dialogue but that society also had a role. “Security alone cannot solve the problem. We, the society and the people, should also try to restrain any kind of anger,” he said.Separately, Lt Gen Girish Kalia, General Officer Commanding of Spear Corps, visited an Assam Rifles forward post in Manipur on Thursday and reviewed the security situation. He was briefed on the preparedness of troops guarding India-Myanmar border.India shares a 1,643 km border with Myanmar, of which 398 km is in Manipur. Fencing has started, and nearly 55 km has been completed in the state. Govt plans to finish it by 2028. Hilly, forested terrain and resistance from militant outfits that use the border to move between the two countries are slowing the work.
Article Summary: A Kuki-Zo woman was killed and her husband injured in an alleged ambush by suspected Naga militants in Manipur’s Kamjong district. Two other members of the community were reported missing as ethnic violence continued in the state. The attack came five days after nine people were killed across three districts, including two Kukis and six Naga men.

Article Title: Wall Street stocks fall as tech selloff weighs on S&P 500, Nasdaq
Article Text:
Technology and chip stocks dragged the Nasdaq down 1.3% and the S&P 500 0.61%

Wall Street's main stock indexes were lower on Friday, as renewed selling in technology and chip stocks weighed on the broader market amid concerns over rising borrowing costs and debt-funded investments in artificial intelligence (AI).The S&P 500 fell 0.61%, while the Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.3%, putting both indexes on track for weekly losses. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was nearly flat, up 0.01%, and headed for a weekly gain, Reuters reported.Technology stocks remained under pressure as investors reassessed the financing behind the AI infrastructure boom. CoreWeave shares fell 9% on Friday and were on track to lose nearly 23% for the week, amid growing scrutiny of the funding required for large-scale AI infrastructure investments."We're starting to see some cracks in the financing of data centers because you're not too sure who's going to be the winners," Tom Plumb, portfolio manager at Plumb Balanced Fund, told Reuters.Concerns over inflation and the prospect of higher interest rates have also unsettled markets. Stronger-than-expected US consumer and wholesale inflation data this week prompted traders to increase bets on further Federal Reserve rate hikes.Meanwhile, US Treasury yields eased on Friday as bond markets stabilised following a rush towards safe-haven assets in the previous session. The yield on the benchmark 10-year Treasury note stood at 5.085%, according to Reuters.Among individual stocks, Micron Technology, Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom and Intel declined, while gains in financial stocks helped limit broader market losses.Elsewhere, Brent crude futures rose 0.85% to $106.83 per barrel, supported by concerns over oil supplies amid heightened tensions in the Middle East and disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz.
Article Summary: Nasdaq down 1.3%, S&P 500 0.61%, Dow Jones Industrial Average 0.01%. Concerns over rising borrowing costs and debt-funded investments in AI. Brent crude futures rise 0.85% to $106.83 per barrel, supported by concerns over oil supplies.

Article Title: US seeks bids to exchange 17 million barrels of crude from strategic reserve
Article Text:
The US Department of Energy has invited bids for an exchange of up to 17 million barrels as Washington seeks to ease pressure on oil supplies amid the Iran war.

The United States is preparing to offer up to 17 million barrels of crude oil from its Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) as Washington steps up efforts to ease pressure on fuel prices amid disruptions caused by the war with Iran.The US Department of Energy on Friday issued a request for proposals for the latest exchange, under which companies would borrow crude from the emergency stockpile and return oil at a later date, reported Reuters.The move forms part of a broader international effort announced in March to stabilise energy markets after the conflict disrupted oil supplies and sent prices higher.At the time, Washington committed to making 172 million barrels available from its strategic reserves as part of a coordinated International Energy Agency (IEA) initiative involving around 30 countries. The wider arrangement aimed to release 400 million barrels of emergency oil stocks worldwide.However, an earlier attempt to offer the remaining barrels under the US commitment met with limited demand from energy companies.In June, companies agreed to borrow only about 500,000 barrels after being required to return additional crude equivalent to premiums of up to 24 per cent, raising questions about the attractiveness of the exchange terms.The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) is the country's emergency stockpile of crude oil, maintained to help cushion supply disruptions and stabilise energy markets during crises. Under an exchange programme, companies can borrow oil from the reserve and return it later, usually with additional barrels as a premium.The latest proposal follows other attempts to increase global fuel supplies. Earlier this month, Trump reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to allow Russian diesel exports, with an initial 300,000 tonnes expected to be released. The move drew criticism from Ukraine and European leaders, who warned that easing restrictions could benefit Moscow financially.Separately, G7 leaders announced on October 2 that they would implement a coordinated release of 100 million barrels of emergency oil stocks through the IEA over four months. The plan included an accelerated release of diesel supplies to address shortages in international markets.Despite these measures, energy markets remain under strain. Brent crude was trading around $106 a barrel on Friday, with continuing attacks on Gulf shipping and disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz keeping supply concerns elevated.
Article Summary: The US Department of Energy has invited bids for an exchange of up to 17 million barrels of crude oil from its Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The move forms part of a broader international effort announced in March to stabilise energy markets after the war with Iran.

Article Title: Russia begins diesel exports after Trump deal amid global oil market concerns
Article Text:
Russian diesel reaches global markets after Trump deal, Kremlin says (representative image)

Russian diesel shipments resume

Ukraine, European officials criticise deal

Kremlin accuses Kyiv of undermining peace efforts

Russian diesel has begun reaching global markets following an agreement with US President Donald Trump, the Kremlin said on Thursday, adding that the supplies could help stabilise oil markets but would not be sufficient to fully achieve that goal."The diesel has started reaching global markets and is expected to have a positive effect on stabilising oil markets, although it will not be enough to fully stabilize them," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters, according to Reuters.Trump said last week that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets to help lower fuel prices. Moscow subsequently partially lifted its ban on diesel exports from October 10 following the agreement.Data from financial information provider LSEG showed on Wednesday that Russia had resumed diesel export loadings from the Baltic port of Primorsk.According to the shipping data cited by Reuters, a tanker carrying around 40,000 metric tonnes of ultra-low sulphur diesel was loaded on October 13 and was heading towards Morocco.Trump said on Friday that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tonnes, or 2.25 million barrels, of diesel to US and global markets.He also said another 500,000 tonnes would be supplied in November, followed by a further 1 million tonnes "immediately thereafter".However, the initial volume would amount to less than a day's supply for the US transport sector alone.US Energy Information Administration data puts daily consumption in the sector at around 2.94 million barrels. The additional volumes announced by Trump would amount to less than four days of demand for US transport.Trump is seeking to bring down US diesel prices ahead of the country's midterm elections on November 3.The agreement has drawn strong criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, European officials and some Republican politicians in Trump's own party.Russia, meanwhile, has rejected European criticism of the diesel arrangement as "cynical", arguing that European countries continue to purchase some Russian oil and liquefied natural gas.The deal comes amid tensions over efforts to secure an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine.Separately, the Kremlin said on Thursday that Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries were running counter to US efforts to initiate peace talks, following a drone attack on a refinery in Russia's Ryazan region overnight.Peskov said Moscow did not believe Kyiv had complied with the energy ceasefire announced by Trump on Sunday. Ukraine had said it paused strikes on Russian oil refineries for three days but resumed them after Russia continued attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure."The Ukrainian regime in Kyiv continues to strike these facilities, thereby, of course, coming into serious contradiction with the peace efforts of the United States and of the American negotiators who are indeed making very vigorous efforts to somehow initiate the peace process. But so far, these vigorous attempts have been thwarted by the unwillingness of the Kyiv regime – and of (President Volodymyr) Zelenskyy personally – to make peace," Peskov said.The news agency Associated Press (AP) reported that the drone strike started a fire at the Ryazan refinery, around 300 kilometres southeast of Moscow. A senior Ukrainian official confirmed that Ukraine had hit the facility, while Russia's Defence Ministry and regional governor reported the attack.Russia had previously said the scope of the energy ceasefire had not been defined. On Wednesday, it said it had struck seven Ukrainian energy infrastructure facilities, according to Reuters.The competing claims over compliance with the ceasefire could not be independently verified.Meanwhile, Zelenskyy said Russia had launched more than 850 drones at Ukraine between midnight and Thursday morning.Ukraine's Emergency Services said three people were killed and six injured in a Russian drone attack on the central Kirovohrad region, while the Ukrainian Air Force said its air defences had intercepted 536 Russian drones during the overnight assault.
Article Summary: Russian diesel has begun reaching global markets following an agreement with US President Donald Trump, the Kremlin says. Trump said last week that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets to help lower fuel prices. Moscow subsequently partially lifted its ban on diesel exports from October 10.

Article Title: Oil prices fall $1 after touching three week high amid Middle East tensions
Article Text:
Crude prices steady after touching three week high

Oil prices fell by more than $1 in early trade on Thursday as investors weighed threats to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz against the possibility of the US easing sanctions on oil-carrying vessels.Brent crude dropped 1.30% to $104.70, shedding $1.38, while West Texas Intermediate (WTI) fell 1.07% to $94.07, a decline of $1.02.The decline followed a sharp rise in WTI in the previous session, when prices reached a three-week high. The rally came after the Houthis attacked Saudi Aramco's headquarters and Iran announced new tactics to target vessels passing through the Strait of Hormuz, with the stated aim of keeping oil prices high.The threat to maritime traffic remained elevated. Two vessels: a container ship and a dry bulk carrier, sank near the strait within 24 hours after separate projectile strikes, maritime officials said on Wednesday.Attacks in the surrounding waters have increased over the past 10 days. Iran has said it is intensifying its strikes in retaliation for the US blockade of Iranian ports and the tougher sanctions imposed last month.The disruption caused by the Iran war has pushed freight costs to record highs, prompting the Trump administration to consider easing restrictions on vessels used to transport oil from sanctioned countries.A US official said on Wednesday that the administration was considering sanctions relief for so-called shadow fleet vessels, which have carried oil and petroleum products from countries including Russia, Iran and Venezuela. The move is aimed at helping reduce petroleum shipping costs.Furthermore, rising oil production and exports from Russia and the Middle East have also helped contain prices amid the supply concerns.Russia's crude oil output increased by 65,000 barrels per day in September to 8.43 million barrels per day, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).However, production remained 870,000 barrels per day lower than a year earlier.The IEA also reported a monthly increase of 4.4 million barrels per day in crude oil exports from Middle East Gulf producers in September. Exports reached around 75% of their prewar levels.Now, the US-Iran conflict has continued for over seven months, keeping oil markets on edge. However, the price spike is far lower than the $126 per barrel levels seen earlier in the crisis.
Article Summary: Brent crude dropped 1.30% to $104.70, shedding $1.38, while West Texas Intermediate (WTI) fell 1.07%. The decline followed a sharp rise in WTI in the previous session, when prices reached a three-week high. The rally came after Iran announced new tactics to target vessels passing through the Strait of Hormuz.

Article Title: US stocks fall as inflation accelerates; S&P 500 drops 1.1%, Nasdaq slides 1.6%
Article Text:
Investors also weighed the risks and potential returns of heavy investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure.

Wall Street stocks fell on Wednesday as hotter-than-expected US inflation data pushed Treasury yields higher, adding to concerns about borrowing costs even as major banks assessed the opportunities and risks associated with the artificial intelligence (AI) investment boom.The S&P 500 fell 1.1%, putting it on track for its fifth decline in six sessions since hitting a record high. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 171 points, or 0.3%, while the Nasdaq Composite declined 1.6%, as of 1:14 pm Eastern time.US consumer prices rose 3.7% year on year in September, accelerating from 3.4% in August and exceeding economists’ expectations of 3.6%. The data fuelled concerns that inflation could remain elevated, partly due to rising energy prices amid the war with Iran.The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield climbed to 5.23%, after briefly crossing 5.32% during the session. Higher yields can weigh on equities by increasing borrowing costs and making bonds more attractive relative to stocks.Meanwhile, executives at major US banks highlighted the opportunities presented by AI infrastructure investment, while cautioning that uncertainty over demand, financing costs and returns could create risks.Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon said the long-term demand for capital and computing capacity required by the AI ecosystem remained uncertain.“No one knows how the demands for capital and compute will evolve as the broader AI ecosystem matures,” Solomon said, stressing the need for vigilance in financing decisions and risk management.Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser, however, said investment in the broader AI ecosystem was not slowing, citing an ongoing shortage of computing capacity.The AI infrastructure expansion, driven by heavy investment in data centres and computing power, presents banks with opportunities to finance large-scale projects. However, elevated interest rates could raise project costs, squeeze returns and make debt repayment more difficult.Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf described the AI buildout as a significant economic force, bringing both opportunities and risks because of the substantial borrowing involved and pressure on prices across some industries and supply chains.Banks are also deploying AI internally to improve productivity and reduce costs, although the financial benefits vary. Fraser said Citi was developing products up to 40% faster using AI and had reduced technology vendor expenses by 30% through coding tools.Investors are watching whether such efficiency gains can justify the heavy spending on AI. Concerns are also mounting over cybersecurity threats and the risks posed by AI agents capable of taking actions autonomously.The combination of persistent inflation, elevated bond yields and uncertainty over AI investment returns has added to the challenges facing Wall Street, where high stock valuations leave limited room for corporate earnings or productivity gains to disappoint.
Article Summary: US consumer prices rose 3.7% year on year in September, accelerating from 3.4% in August and exceeding economists’ expectations of 3.6%. The data fuelled concerns that inflation could remain elevated, partly due to rising energy prices amid the war with Iran. Investors also weighed the risks and potential returns of heavy investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure.

Article Title: US inflation accelerates to 3.7% in September as gasoline prices surge
Article Text:
This the sharpest increase in five months, as higher fuel costs and persistent underlying price pressures added to the cost-of-living burden

Gasoline prices drive inflation

Core inflation also picks up

What it means for Federal Reserve

US consumer inflation accelerated in September as a surge in gasoline prices and firmer underlying price pressures added to the cost-of-living burden for American households ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.The consumer price index (CPI) rose 3.7 per cent year-on-year in September, up from 3.4 per cent in August, the US Labor Department said on Wednesday. On a monthly basis, consumer prices increased 0.6 per cent, compared with a 0.4 per cent rise in the previous month.The annual inflation rate was slightly above economists' expectations of 3.6 per cent, according to a Reuters poll, while the monthly increase was in line with forecasts.The latest figures reflect the impact of higher energy costs following the US-Israeli war with Iran, which began in late February and disrupted oil and gas supplies. Rising costs have added to concerns over affordability, a key issue ahead of the midterm elections, in which President Donald Trump's Republican Party is seeking to retain control of Congress.Gasoline prices were a major contributor to the monthly increase in consumer prices, rising sharply in September.US Energy Information Administration data showed gasoline prices climbed 7.1 per cent during the month, while the Labor Department's CPI report recorded a 9.1 per cent increase.Higher fuel costs have also pushed up expenses across other sectors, including transportation and travel. Airfares rose 1.2 per cent in September and were up around 22 per cent from a year earlier, while hotel prices increased 2 per cent over the month.Rising fuel and transportation expenses have also increased costs for businesses, raising the risk that companies will pass some of the additional burden on to consumers through higher prices for goods and services.Grocery prices offered some relief, declining 0.1 per cent in September, although they remained 1.8 per cent higher than a year earlier.Underlying price pressures remained firm even after excluding volatile food and energy components. Core CPI rose 2.6 per cent in September from a year earlier, compared with 2.4 per cent in August.On a monthly basis, core inflation increased 0.3 per cent, matching the previous month's rise. Price increases across a range of goods and services suggest that inflationary pressures extend beyond the energy sector.Economists have also pointed to strong investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure and data centres as a factor pushing up the cost of semiconductors, computer equipment and electronic devices.“The report was worse than expected,” Bill Adams, chief US economist at Fifth Third Bank, said in a note to clients, adding that price increases were widespread across durable goods, nondurable goods and services.The inflation data could complicate the Federal Reserve's decisions on interest rates as policymakers weigh persistent price pressures against the impact of tighter monetary policy on economic growth.The Fed raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points last month to a range of 3.75 per cent to 4 per cent, marking its first rate increase in three years. It has indicated that further increases could follow if inflation remains elevated.Financial markets had assigned a roughly 22 per cent probability of another rate increase at the Fed's October 27-28 meeting before the September CPI report, according to CME Group's FedWatch Tool.However, some economists expect policymakers to hold rates steady at the upcoming meeting and assess further economic data before deciding on another increase. Higher borrowing costs can help moderate demand and slow price increases, but they cannot directly address supply disruptions caused by geopolitical conflicts.The latest inflation figures come as the cost of living remains a major concern for American voters ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.The September inflation report is also important for millions of Americans receiving Social Security benefits. The annual cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 is based on inflation data for urban wage earners and clerical workers during the third quarter of 2026 compared with the corresponding period a year earlier.The Senior Citizens League has projected a 3.5 per cent increase in Social Security benefits for 2027, up from the 2.8 per cent adjustment for 2026. The Social Security Administration is expected to announce the official adjustment later on Wednesday.
Article Summary: Consumer price index (CPI) rose 3.7 per cent year-on-year in September, up from 3.4 per cent in August. On a monthly basis, consumer prices increased 0.6 per cent, compared with a 0.4% rise in the previous month. Rising costs have added to concerns over affordability, a key issue ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

Article Title: 'Making progress': Taiwan on Alaska LNG deal after Trump says it will buy 30% of output
Article Text:
Taiwan advances Alaska LNG deal.

Taiwan said on Wednesday it was making progress in negotiations to buy liquefied natural gas (LNG) from Alaska and planned to invest up to $4.4 billion in the project. The announcement came after US President Donald Trump said Taiwan had agreed to buy 30% of the proposed project's output.Taiwan's economy ministry said state-owned energy company CPC Corp had made significant progress with the project developer after nearly 18 months of negotiations and evaluation.Under the plan, CPC would purchase 6 million metric tonnes of LNG annually once production begins, in line with a letter of intent signed last year.The company would also participate in the project's development, with an estimated investment of up to $4.4 billion, the ministry said, Reuters reported."Specific investment arrangements, equity stakes and related terms will be determined through subsequent negotiations and commercial contract procedures," it added.However, the final investment terms and purchase commitments remain subject to further negotiations and commercial agreements.Taiwan has been looking to increase purchases of US natural gas and reduce its dependence on other suppliers. Earlier in February, officials said US gas would account for about one-third of the island's imported supply this year.The proposed Alaska LNG project is designed to export up to 20 million metric tonnes of LNG annually. The project has been discussed for decades, but its commercial viability remains a concern for some industry experts.If completed, the pipeline would provide a direct route for US LNG to Asian markets, including Taiwan, without requiring shipments to pass through the Panama Canal or travel around the Horn of Africa. This could reduce shipping times and costs.The move is also part of Taiwan's effort to narrow its large trade surplus with the United States, which has angered the Trump administration.CPC signed an agreement with the Alaska Gasline Development Corporation last year to buy LNG and invest in the project. Alaska's governor said in March 2025 that Taiwan had signed a letter of intent to purchase 6 million metric tonnes annually.Taiwan President Lai Ching-te had said the investment would help strengthen the island's energy security.Last year, Taiwan Presidential Office Secretary-General Pan Men-an also visited the proposed project site in Alaska as the Trump administration promoted the project to Asian allies.Trump at a rally in Alaska on Tuesday said that Taiwan had agreed to buy 30% of the project's output.US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who attended the event organised by the Republican National Committee, said Taiwan had committed $4.4 billion towards the pipeline's development.Taiwan Premier Cho Jung-tai, responding to Trump's remarks said the government's responsibility was to "stabilize the entire energy supply and build its resilience, like governments everywhere."The announcement did not establish whether a final, binding agreement had been signed. Taiwan's economy ministry said the investment arrangements and equity stakes would be settled through further negotiations.Last month, Trump said South Korea had agreed to invest in the Alaska LNG project, which he valued at $54 billion. Seoul, however, said the proposed investment had not yet been finalised.
Article Summary: Taiwan says it is making progress in negotiations to buy liquefied natural gas (LNG) from Alaska. Announcement came after US President Donald Trump said Taiwan had agreed to buy 30% of the proposed project's output. Taiwan has been looking to increase purchases of US natural gas and reduce its dependence on other suppliers.

Article Title: From Chinese money laundering to Russia, Iran sanctions - why was Bank of America fined $1.21 billion?
Article Text:
File photo: US Treasury Department announced a $1.2 billion fine against Bank of America for violating anti-money laundering laws

Violated Bank Secrecy Act

Bank of America has been fined $1.21 billion by US regulators for failing to detect and report billions of dollars in suspicious transactions, including activity linked to potential money laundering and sanctions violations.The US treasury department said the bank failed to report more than $5 billion in suspicious activity, including $1 billion that posed national security-related and other illicit finance risks. The unreported activity included transactions that may have involved Chinese money laundering networks and trade-based laundering linked to the US southwest border, according to the Treasury.The department said the bank prioritised revenue while building its compliance programmes and relied too heavily on inquiries from law enforcement and other financial institutions rather than its own internal controls. This effectively outsourced a substantial part of its responsibility to proactively detect and report suspicious activity, it said.As part of the settlement, Bank of America admitted that it had “willfully violated” the Bank Secrecy Act by failing to maintain a compliant anti-money laundering programme, conduct required due diligence on foreign correspondent accounts and file suspicious activity reports, the Treasury said.The $1.21 billion penalty includes a $750 million civil fine imposed by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), the largest in the regulator’s history. The OCC said the bank had failed to address shortcomings in its anti-money laundering programmes identified in a 2024 cease-and-desist order. It described the bank’s compliance programme as “deficient and ineffective” and said its transaction monitoring system had delayed reports covering billions of dollars in transactions.The bank also agreed to pay $11.6 million to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) over 475 apparent violations of sanctions programmes targeting Russia, Iran, narcotics and global terrorism. OFAC said the settlement reflected its determination that the apparent violations were “non-egregious”.Under the settlement, the bank must hire an independent third party to review past transactions, identify suspicious activity it failed to detect and report those transactions to the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN).Bank of America said it had invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to fighting financial crime. It added that it was committed to completing the work required by regulators and had already devoted substantial personnel and resources to remediation.The bank said its third-quarter results, due on Wednesday, would include a non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2 billion, reducing net income by approximately 17 cents per share.The penalty comes days after American Express was fined $350 million for similar anti-money laundering shortcomings. Bank of America shares fell 2.7% in after-hours trading on Tuesday, after closing down 1.1%.
Article Summary: Bank failed to report more than $5 billion in suspicious activity, including $1 billion that posed national security-related and other illicit finance risks. The $1.21 billion penalty includes a $750 million civil fine imposed by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.

Article Title: Oil prices climb as Houthis step up attacks on Saudi Arabia, stoking supply fears
Article Text:
Oil prices rise to to $106.58 a barrel (AI-generated image)

Oil prices rose on Wednesday as traders weighed the risk of supply disruptions from escalating attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia against expectations of increased Russian diesel exports easing market tightness.Brent crude futures rose 89 cents, or 0.8%, to $106.58 a barrel by 0030 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures gained 80 cents, or 0.9%, to $94.94. Brent had fallen 0.9% on Tuesday, while WTI gained 0.4%.“Supply concern stemming from conflict between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia is driving prices higher,” Hiroyuki Kikukawa, chief strategist at Nissan Securities Investment, told Reuters. He said expectations of increased Russian diesel exports could limit sharp price movements in either direction.Saudi Arabia’s energy ministry said the Houthis attacked an administrative building belonging to state-owned oil company Saudi Aramco in Dhahran, causing a limited fire. The group has launched ballistic missiles and drones at the kingdom over the past week in retaliation for Riyadh’s support for Yemeni government forces.US president Donald Trump accused the Houthis of deliberately trying to drive up oil prices ahead of the US midterm elections.In a post on Truth Social on Tuesday, he said the group had re-emerged, probably at Iran’s behest, and warned that he would not forget the attacks after the elections.Trump also threatened to step up US military action in the Middle East after the November elections, which will determine whether Republicans retain their majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate.Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia increased oil production last month despite disruptions to shipments caused by the US-Iran war, contributing to a sharp rise in output from OPEC+, the oil producers’ alliance, according to data cited by Reuters.Iran is also deploying new tactics to target ships in the Strait of Hormuz in an effort to keep oil prices high and influence the US midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters.In a potential counterweight to supply concerns, Russia said on Tuesday it saw no direct link between peace talks with Ukraine and its deal to export diesel to the US. The statement followed a report that US envoys had told Ukrainian officials the deal was part of an effort to bring Moscow back to negotiations.Analysts expect the competing pressures from regional conflict and potential increases in fuel supply to shape oil price movements in the coming days.
Article Summary: Brent crude futures rose 89 cents, or 0.8%, to $106.58 a barrel by 0030 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate crude futures gained 80 cents, to $94.94 a barrel. Brent had fallen 0.9% on Tuesday, while WTI gained 0.4%.

Article Title: Wall Street mixed as bank earnings lift Goldman, Iran war and inflation weigh
Article Text:
The S&P 500 fell 0.1 per cent, the Dow Jones dropped 190 points or 0.4 per cent, and the Nasdaq Composite declined 0.2 per cent.

Trading revenue supports bank earnings

Wall Street stocks traded mixed on Tuesday as investors assessed a fresh batch of corporate earnings, with strong results from major US banks offset by concerns over market volatility, inflation and the economic fallout of the Iran war.The S&P 500 slipped 0.1 per cent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 190 points, or 0.4 per cent, and the Nasdaq Composite declined 0.2 per cent. The moves came as the benchmark indexes remained close to their record levels, with investors weighing whether companies can sustain their profit growth amid rising borrowing costs and geopolitical uncertainty.Goldman Sachs shares recovered to trade 0.3 per cent higher after initially jumping more than 4 per cent following a stronger-than-expected quarterly profit. The bank benefited from robust equities trading, although revenue from its fixed income, currencies and commodities business fell 1 per cent from a year earlier.Chief executive David Solomon said the economy remained resilient despite several headwinds. "The economy continues to be very, very resilient despite some of the headwinds," he said, pointing to a strong technology investment cycle and a regulatory environment encouraging corporate activity.Banking activity faces late-quarter slowdownResults from JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup, Goldman Sachs and Wells Fargo indicated that the dealmaking and trading momentum seen in the first half of the year may have moderated towards the end of the third quarter. Executives cited volatile equity markets, rising bond yields and uncertainty surrounding the economic outlook as factors weighing on investment banking activity.JPMorgan said market turbulence had slowed dealmaking and affected bond trading, particularly during the second half of September. However, chief financial officer Jeremy Barnum said the pipeline of potential deals remained "very strong", with many transactions delayed rather than cancelled.Goldman Sachs chief Solomon also expressed optimism about future activity, saying the initial public offering (IPO) market remained in good shape despite a recent loss of momentum. Companies could postpone listings until market conditions improve, he said.Citigroup chief financial officer Gonzalo Luchetti reported softer investment banking activity during the quarter, while Wells Fargo finance chief Mike Santomassimo also pointed to a slowdown in September as benchmark bond yields rose sharply."There is no doubt that high interest rates and the threat of continued Fed hikes is weighing on trading and IB activity in a measurably negative vector," said Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management.Equities trading remained a bright spot for major banks as clients adjusted their portfolios amid uncertainty over interest rates and rising energy prices. JPMorgan reported a 15 per cent increase in revenue from its markets division in the third quarter compared with a year earlier, while equities markets revenue surged 49 per cent.Goldman also exceeded analysts' profit expectations, supported by stronger equities trading linked to volatility surrounding the Middle East conflict. Its fixed income, currencies and commodities business, however, recorded a year-on-year decline in revenue.JPMorgan shares rose 0.1 per cent after fluctuating between gains and losses, while Wells Fargo fell 1.8 per cent following weaker-than-expected revenue despite beating profit estimates. Citigroup shares also declined, while Goldman Sachs ended in positive territory.JPMorgan chief executive Jamie Dimon flagged elevated asset prices, persistent inflation, higher interest rates and geopolitical tensions as risks to the economic outlook. "These forces may be manageable, but we remain prepared for a wide range of outcomes," he said.Despite these concerns, bank executives said consumers and corporate borrowers remained resilient, with limited signs of deterioration in credit quality. Santomassimo said Wells Fargo was not seeing indications of significant financial stress among borrowers.Markets weigh earnings against wider risksBeyond the banking sector, technology stocks remained under pressure amid concerns about valuations and competition in the artificial intelligence industry. Micron Technology fell 5.1 per cent after reports that Chinese memory-chip maker CXMT was making advances that could challenge established players, including Micron, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. South Korea's Kospi index dropped 5.5 per cent.Bumble shares surged 56.2 per cent after the dating-app company agreed to a $1.3 billion all-cash buyout by Ithaca Holdings.In the bond market, the yield on the US 10-year Treasury eased to 5.22 per cent from 5.24 per cent late Friday, while oil prices declined. Brent crude fell 0.5 per cent to $106.11 a barrel as uncertainty over the Iran war continued to influence energy markets.The broader earnings outlook remains strong, with analysts forecasting nearly 30 per cent year-on-year profit growth for S&P 500 companies in the third quarter, according to FactSet. However, investors remain focused on whether corporate results can justify elevated stock valuations amid inflationary pressures, rising bond yields and geopolitical risks.Chris Kotowski, an analyst at Oppenheimer & Co, cautioned that much of the banks' earnings outperformance appeared to be concentrated in equities trading, raising questions about whether the gains could be sustained.
Article Summary: The S&P 500 slipped 0.1 per cent, the Dow Jones dropped 190 points or 0.4 per cent and the Nasdaq Composite declined 0.2 per cent. Goldman Sachs shares recovered to trade 0.3 per cent higher after initially jumping more than 4 per cent following a stronger-than-expected quarterly profit.

Article Title: Oil prices hold near $105 per barrel as Trump eases sanctions on Russian fuel
Article Text:
Crude holds near $105 per barrel

Oil prices edged lower on Tuesday after rising by nearly $2 a barrel in the previous session, as traders weighed the risks to supplies from attacks on Saudi Arabia against the prospect of additional diesel supplies from Russia.West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude was trading at $92.84 a barrel, down $0.90, or 0.96%, while Brent crude fell $1.01, or 0.95%, to $105.60 a barrel. This comes after Brent futures had settled at $106.65 a barrel on Monday, their highest level since September 15.Oil markets have found some relief after US President Donald Trump said that Russia has agreed to supply diesel to global markets. The US administation temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel, which were designed to deprive Moscow of revenue for its war on Ukraine.These additional supplies could ease tightness in global fuel markets and temper some of the supply concerns that have supported crude prices in recent weeks.However, lawmakers from both parties in the US complained that Trump's agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin appeared to violate US law barring imports of Russian energy until Moscow ends its aggression against Ukraine.Concerns about the vulnerability of energy infrastructure and shipping lanes in the Gulf continued to weigh on market sentiment after Iran-aligned Houthis struck Riyadh's international airport over the weekend.Attacks on tankers were also reported near the Strait of Hormuz.The incidents threatened to derail the recovery in Middle East supplies seen in September, reinforcing concerns about further disruptions along one of the world's most important energy transit routes.Ministers of OPEC and non-OPEC Participating Countries in the Declaration of Cooperation said shipping and insurance costs had surged to unprecedented levels, exceeding one-third of the commodity value. The higher costs were impeding the efficient movement of crude oil and petroleum products.OPEC has also lowered its forecast for oil demand growth this year to 400,000 barrels per day (bpd), from 1.4 million bpd at the start of the year, reflecting developments throughout the year, the organisation's secretary general, Haitham Al Ghais, said on Monday, as cited by Reuters.Meanwhile, Goldman Sachs said that brent crude prices could fall to the $60s per barrel in 2027 if oil production in the Persian Gulf recovers faster than expected. However, the investment bank warned that further escalation in the region could push prices significantly higher.The bank said Brent could decline to the $60s if average oil output in the Gulf in 2027 rises by 1 million bpd above February 2026 levels.“A faster recovery in Mideast output and/or a faster erosion of the risk premium are the most likely potential triggers of price downside,” Goldman Sachs said.Continued adjustments in Middle East oil supplies would eventually bring crude prices down but renewed escalation in the region remained a significant risk that could push prices higher.Now, the Middle East conflict has continued disrupt energy supplies for over seven months now, rattling oil markets and pushing prices high. However, even with the ongoing tensions, the spike is far lower than the $126 per barrel seen earlier during the crisis.
Article Summary: West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude was trading at $92.84 a barrel, down $0.90. Brent crude fell $1.01, or 0.95%, to $105.60 a barrel. Brent futures had settled at $106.65 a barrel on Monday, their highest level since September 15.

Article Title: Dow rises, S&P 500 near record as Wall Street braces for key US data
Article Text:
Wall Street opened the week on a mixed note, with energy stocks gaining

Wall Street stocks traded mixed on Monday, with the S&P 500 holding near its record high as gains in energy shares offset losses in technology stocks. Investors also turned their attention to a fresh round of corporate earnings and key US inflation data due later this week.The S&P 500 rose 0.1%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 0.4%, adding 228 points. The Nasdaq Composite slipped 0.2%, reflecting pressure on some of the technology stocks that have helped drive the market's gains this year.Energy shares advanced as crude oil prices climbed amid concerns over global supplies. Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose 2% to $106.77 per barrel. Oil prices have fluctuated sharply in recent weeks amid uncertainty surrounding the US war with Iran and its implications for energy supplies and inflation. Chevron gained 1.4%.Technology stocks were among the biggest drags on the market, with Micron Technology falling 2.8% and Advanced Micro Devices declining 2.4%. Investors are looking for evidence that the surge in artificial intelligence-related investment will translate into sustained earnings growth and justify the sector's strong stock-market performance.Artificial intelligence continues to support the outlook for technology companies and their suppliers, but questions remain over the longer-term returns from the technology.As companies begin reporting quarterly results, investors will be watching whether earnings can sustain the momentum behind market valuations.Oil prices remain another key variable for markets. Rising crude costs can push up petrol and diesel prices, increase transportation expenses and feed into the cost of goods. This could complicate the Federal Reserve's efforts to bring inflation down to its 2% target.Investors will get fresh readings on price pressures and consumer demand this week. The US consumer price index (CPI), due on Wednesday, is expected to show annual inflation rising to 3.6% in September from 3.4% in August. Producer price inflation and retail sales data are scheduled for Thursday, offering further insight into business costs and household spending.The data could influence expectations for the Federal Reserve's interest-rate decisions. Persistent inflation has kept the prospect of further rate increases in focus, while higher bond yields have raised borrowing costs across the economy. The 10-year US Treasury yield recently touched its highest level since 2002 before easing to 5.24% late Friday. US bond markets were closed on Monday for the Columbus Day holiday.The housing market will also be in focus, as elevated mortgage rates weigh on affordability and demand. Investors are due to receive an update on home sales on Tuesday.Meanwhile, the latest earnings season gathers pace with results from major US banks. Citigroup, JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo are scheduled to report on Tuesday, followed by Bank of America on Wednesday. Their results are expected to provide clues about lending activity, consumer finances and the broader economic outlook.Elsewhere, European markets advanced, while most Asian markets ended lower. Tokyo markets were closed for a holiday.
Article Summary: The S&P 500 rose 0.1%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 0.4%. The Nasdaq Composite slipped 0.2%, reflecting pressure on some of the technology stocks that have helped drive the market's gains this year. Energy shares advanced as crude oil prices climbed amid concerns over global supplies.

Article Title: 1.14 lakh startups generate more than 12 lakh jobs in India: Finance ministry
Article Text:
Finance Ministry

NEW DELHI: More than 1.14 lakh startups in India have created over 12 lakh jobs so far, the finance ministry said in its latest review of the Indian economy.In the report titled, ‘The Indian Economy: A Review January 2024’, the Department of Economic Affairs said that the 1.14 lakh startups recognised by the government under the 'Startup India initiative’ created more than 12 lakh jobs (as of October 2023).The state-owned e-commerce platform Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC) clocked more than 63 lakh transactions till November 2023, the document read.Despite facing global challenges in 2023 like valuation issues, few IPOs, regulatory changes and macroeconomic and geopolitical trends, India remains the third largest tech start-up ecosystem globally, with over 950 tech startups founded last year.The cumulative funding for more than 31,000 tech start ups has exceeded $70 billion (from 2019 to 2023), according to a recent report by Nasscom in collaboration with Zinnov.“In 2023, despite facing global economic and regulatory challenges, Indian tech startups have prioritised the imperative of enhancing their business fundamentals, driving profitability and growth,” said Debjani Ghosh, President, Nasscom.“The proliferation of tech startups in tier 2 and 3 cities marks the ecosystem's resilience,” she added.Navigating 2024, tech startup founders expect to continue the revenue growth path with measured steps focusing on optimising expenditure and maximising profitability for B2B tech startups.Investments in deeptech will continue an upward trend in 2024. With generative AI (GenAI) acceleration, 70 per cent of start-up founders are embedding artificial intelligence (AI) in their solutions.As funding becomes scarce for the Indian startup ecosystem in general, the explosion of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has given a new lease of life to entrepreneurs and founders in the country, as the Centre extends support to the sector.
Article Summary: The state-owned e-commerce platform Open Network for Digital Commerce clocked more than 63 lakh transactions till November 2023. India remains the third largest tech start-up ecosystem globally, with over 950 tech startups founded last year. The cumulative funding for more than 31,000 tech start ups has exceeded $70 billion.

Article Title: Startups Revolutionizing Carbon Dioxide into Valuable Products
Article Text: For most perfume makers, ingredients to make it smell great are the most important feature. But for Stafford Sheehan, a cofounder and chemist at Air Company, the most important part of perfume-making has no scent at all.New York-based Air Company uses technology that converts planet-warming carbon dioxide into ethanol, which is then blended with essential oils and water to produce perfume. While the pale yellow-color Air Eau de Parfum is about 50% more expensive than Coco Chanel’s signature No. 5, Sheehan says his product is uniquely valuable: Every 50-milliliter bottle uses 3.6 grams of CO2 that otherwise would have been released into the atmosphere. Its package reads: “Turning CO2 into something beautiful.”While the volume of CO2 utilized in the bottle is extremely small, Air Company’s perfume showcases one way the coming wave of captured carbon can be put to use. Renewable energy and electric cars alone won’t be enough to cut CO2 emissions to zero. The world will almost certainly need to capture billions of tons of the gas annually in the coming decades. Large amounts will likely be stored underground.Using it — so-called carbon capture and utilization, or CCU — to create new products from perfume to jet fuel could be an important tool in the fight against climate change, too, though the nascent industry has major hurdles to overcome.Roughly 230 million tons of CO2 are utilized every year, according to a 2019 report by the International Energy Agency. While roughly one-third of that is reused to force more oil from the ground — hardly a carbon-neutral process — CCU advocates say that the number of companies coming up with new uses for carbon has mushroomed in recent years, paving a way to unlock climate benefits. Carbon-derived fuels and chemicals, for example, could theoretically grow to the scale of billions of tons of CO2 use per year if companies could perfect their technology and lower costs.Calgary-based CleanO2 transforms CO2 captured from building heating boilers into feedstock to make soap. Newlight Technologies, a biotechnology startup based in California, takes carbon pulled directly from the air and turns it into biodegradable plastics. Germany’s Covestro AG, one of the world’s largest polymer manufacturers, is also switching some of its fossil fuel-based feedstocks to carbon-derived materials for everything ranging from car shells to medical devices and stadium roofs.Most companies working on CO2-sequestering products are still in their infancy. To grow the emerging sector, global venture capitalists in 2022 poured nearly $500 million into carbon utilization businesses, according to the IEA. That’s in stark contrast to 2015, when barely any venture money went to technologies that utilize CO2.“It’s just a whole different landscape today than it was a decade ago,” says Sasha Mackler, executive director of the energy program at Washington, DC-based non-profit Bipartisan Policy Center.Jennifer Holmgren, chief executive officer of LanzaTech Global Inc., has experienced the shifting sentiment firsthand. The Illinois-based company uses a carbon-eating bacteria – discovered in the guts of rabbits and preserved as powder – to make alternative ethanol in bioreactors not dissimilar to how breweries ferment beer. In the early 2010s, when Holmgren touted carbon-derived ethanol to prospective customers, her sales pitch was met with skepticism.But the tide began turning later that decade. In 2018, the company’s jet fuel produced from the emissions of a Chinese steel mill helped power a Transatlantic flight. LanzaTech has also inked agreements with airlines including Japan’s All Nippon Airways to supply CO2-derived jet fuel. And LanzaJet, the company’s spin-off, plans to start producing sustainable jet fuels at a commercial scale this year.Yet for all the hype around sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) using captured carbon, the industry is still an extremely small player. Almost every major airline in the world has pledged to use at least 10% sustainable jet fuels by 2030, yet SAF makes up only 0.1% of global aviation fuel supply — and much of it is made from sources other than captured CO2, such as used cooking oil.“There’s a lot more interest because consumers have become much more interested in buying things that are lower carbon,” says Holmgren. That’s enabled LanzaTech to expand the number of products that utilize CO2.American plastic container maker Plastipak, for instance, has partnered with LanzaTech to produce carbon-derived packaging materials, while polyester converted from LanzaTech’s ethanol has replaced its petroleum-based counterpart at a pilot scale in Lululemon shorts, Zara dresses, H&M yoga pants, On running shoes and Craghoppers jackets. Like SAF, though, there’s still a long way to go for CO2-derived polyester to reach meaningful levels of use.Momentum to grow beyond one-off products and low-scale production has also been supercharged by a growing array of regulations and incentives around the world. For instance, the Inflation Reduction Act that US President Joe Biden signed in 2022 raised the tax credit for carbon capture and utilization by more than 70% to $60 per metric ton in an effort to make costly projects more financially appealing.To keep the climate within habitable limits, the IEA estimates that carbon capture will have to grow to 7.6 billion tons of CO2 annually by mid-century. CCU will play a role, though just how big remains to be seen. Not every use case is created equal and some approaches, such as dissolving compressed CO2 in water to make carbonated beverages, only store the gas temporarily. To quantify the true climate benefit of carbon utilization, experts say third-party verification is badly needed.The rise of CCU technology comes as another key approach in President Biden’s net-zero roadmap is hitting a bit of a wall. Carbon capture and storage — that is, gathering CO2 as it’s released from a coal-fired power plant or other emissions source and sequestering it underground — has faced challenges because carbon is often captured in one place and stored in another. That requires pipelines to transport the gas, which many local communities have opposed. Blackrock-backed Navigator, for example, recently announced it was scrapping a planned 1,300-mile CO2 pipeline.Carbon utilization companies say that they can sidestep that issue by using carbon near or at where it’s captured.At its 12-acre factory in Brooklyn, Glenwood Mason Supply demonstrates how. The concrete manufacturer takes CO2 captured at a residential building by its partner company, CarbonQuest, and uses a technique licensed from low-carbon concrete startup CarbonCure to convert the compressed carbon into a powder not unlike dry ice. It then injects it into industrial mixers. There, the CO2 meets cement, sand and aggregate, setting off a series of chemical reactions. The final result is concrete blocks with CO2 sealed in.The technique not only stores carbon but it can also make the blocks marginally stronger. The company estimates that it has utilized about 100 tons of CO2 in total since 2020. Even if the blocks break down, the stored carbon won’t be released as CO2 because it’s been mineralized.“Cement is a big offender in carbon emissions,” says Constance Cincotta, founder of the concrete factory. She became intrigued by the technology and its ability to lower her company's climate impact after hearing about it at an industry conference in the early 2010s. But it wasn't until CarbonCure came on the scene a few years ago that the prospect of CO2-storing cement became tangible. Glenwood Mason then sourced CO2 locally from CarbonQuest, which captures carbon from buildings in New York. Those factors have enabled large-scale production.While Cincotta’s intended to help the planet, she and her team discovered that sinking CO2 into concrete blocks is good for the business, too. In 2019, New York City — where the majority of the company’s concrete blocks are sold — passed a regulation requiring all buildings to shrink their carbon footprint 40% by the end of the decade. Glenwood Mason’s phones have been ringing ever since, with calls from architects and property developers who want to leverage their lower-carbon building materials to cut emissions, says Jeff Hansen, the company’s vice president in architectural sales and marketing.The factory’s CO2-storing concrete blocks also caught the eye of Amazon.com Inc, which in 2022 persuaded a real estate developer to purchase roughly 50,000 blocks for the construction of a new warehouse in New York that Amazon has leased. Had Glenwood Mason not sealed CO2 in its blocks, it wouldn’t have won the contract, Hansen says. To figure out how to pack more carbon into its products, the company has set up a laboratory in its factory to test the reaction between CO2 and other concrete feedstocks under different temperatures and humidity levels.But figuring out the right formula is only one consideration. Utilizing CO2 often comes with an additional cost. As the demand for CO2-derived products climbs, that green premium is expected to go down. Yet “it’s very hard to be a cost parity with a 100-year-old industry that doesn’t even have to pay for its externalities,” says Holmgren of LanzaTech. Even with economies of scale, Holmgren estimates that carbon-containing fabrics will still likely cost as much as 20% higher than conventional ones.“It’s unlikely that we will ever be a cost parity,” she says.In addition to the cost barrier, CCU companies also have to convince end users that may be suspicious of unproven new technologies.Changing feedstocks “does come with risks,” says Keith Wiggins, chief executive officer of Econic Technologies, a British startup that specializes in making carbon-derived chemicals. To get risk-averse industries onboard, Wiggins says his company is laser-focused on those that are under consumer pressure to change course.That strategy seems to be working. Econic has teamed up with three manufacturers in the US, China and India to produce mattresses, outdoor garments and building insulation materials that utilize CO2. The first batch of products using the company’s technology are scheduled to enter the market in 2024.For all the promise of the carbon utilization industry, it remains to be seen if it can challenge the status quo. While Air Company started selling carbon-derived perfume in 2021, the startup has yet to build its first commercial plant, Sheehan says, citing the time-consuming process needed for collecting data and fine-tuning the technology for large-scale production.Fow now, the company’s demonstration facility in New York City — where CO2 and hydrogen gas flow through tubes into a reactor to form chemical reactions, aided by catalysts made from a confidential mixture of metals — is designed to yield at least 10,000 gallons of CO2-derived liquid annually. The limited production capacity has left many orders for its perfume — as well as jet fuels and Air Vodka, another popular product made from CO2 — unfilled.“We need to scale these facilities to the size of oil refineries today in order to have the impact on climate change that we want to have,” Sheehan says.
Article Summary: New York-based Air Company uses technology that converts planet-warming carbon dioxide into ethanol, which is then blended with essential oils and water to produce perfume. Carbon-derived fuels and chemicals, for example, could theoretically grow to the scale of billions of tons of CO2 use per year if companies could perfect their technology.

Article Title: E-commerce firm Udaan raises $340 million ahead of planned IPO
Article Text: Indian e-commerce firm Udaan raised $340 million to strengthen its supply chain and boost vendor partnerships ahead of a stock market debut planned for 2025.The Series E round was done via a combination of fresh equity and conversion of debt, the Bangalore-based company said in a statement Thursday. The round was led by M&G Plc and existing investors including Lightspeed Venture Partners and DST Global participated.The round “fully funds our business plan,” Vaibhav Gupta, Udaan co-founder and chief executive officer, said in the statement. “It enables our continued journey of growth and profitability, positioning us well to be public-market ready in the next 12-18 months.”Udaan, which competes with Reliance Industries Ltd. and Walmart Inc.’s Flipkart in helping smaller merchants source their goods, runs an online marketplace and logistics networks that help mum-and-pop stores get quicker deliveries and cut traditional middlemen out. That kind of digital-led wholesale business, though a very small part of India’s overall retail market, is expected to swell to $150 billion in sales in a decade, according to McKinsey & Co.The startup targets an initial public offering in 2025, though it’s yet to decide whether it will do so in India or overseas, Gupta told Bloomberg News last month.Udaan was founded in 2016 by three engineers who previously worked at Flipkart. The trio together ran the company until Gupta, one of the founders, took over as CEO in 2021. The other two founders — Amod Malviya and Sujeet Kumar — are board members.
Article Summary: Indian e-commerce firm Udaan raised $340 million to strengthen its supply chain. The Series E round was done via a combination of fresh equity and conversion of debt. The startup targets an initial public offering in 2025, though it’s yet to decide whether it will do so in India or overseas.

Article Title: Minuscule AI startup raises $41 million to tap India growth
Article Text: A generative artificial intelligence startup targeting the Indian market raised $41 million in fresh funding, the largest such round by an early-stage AI contender in the country.Sarvam AI is building large language models targeted at unique uses in Indian languages at price points that the country’s 1.4 billion people can afford. The Series A funding round was led by Lightspeed Venture Partners, and participants included Silicon Valley billionaire Vinod Khosla’s Khosla Ventures and Peak XV Partners, formerly Sequoia Capital India & Southeast Asia, Sarvam said Thursday.The Bangalore-based startup, until recently in stealth mode, was co-founded by Vivek Raghavan and Pratyush Kumar. It has ambitious plans to build open source foundational AI systems as well as tools for creating apps for the meager compute infrastructure available to developers in India. The startup has a total of 18 employees and is just opening an office in the city."What we are showing is that you can build large language models with limited resources,” Raghavan said in a phone interview. "We are building at a smaller scale and demonstrating that these can be extremely cost and energy efficient so they can be accessed by everyone."Large language models, like OpenAI’s GPT-4 and Meta Platforms Inc.’s Llama, are powerful AI systems that understand by learning from vast amounts of diverse data from the internet and elsewhere to summarize, translate, and create text, audio and video for a wide range of applications. The rivalry to develop ever-more sophisticated models is heating up in Silicon Valley and such efforts have attracted billions of dollars in investments.
Article Summary: Sarvam AI is building large language models targeted at unique uses in Indian languages. The Bangalore-based startup, until recently in stealth mode, was co- founded by Vivek Raghavan and Pratyush Kumar. It has ambitious plans to build open source foundational AI systems.

Article Title: ZestMoney set to shut operations this month
Article Text: NEW DELHI: Buy now Pay Later (BNPL) startup ZestMoney has decided to shut operations. The move will impact some 150 employees of the firm, the company's management told employees in a town hall on Tuesday. ZestMoney did not comment. It is learnt that the firm will shut down by the end of this month.The move comes after attempts by the Bengaluru-based startup to get acquired by larger peer PhonePe failed. The deal was called off earlier this year after a due diligence process undertaken by PhonePe, while evaluating the potential acquisition failed to meet its bar. The Walmart-owned fintech major had, however, hired some 130 of ZestMoney's employees.
Article Summary: The move will impact some 150 employees of the firm, the company's management told employees in a town hall on Tuesday. The move comes after attempts by the Bengaluru-based startup to get acquired by larger peer PhonePe failed. The Walmart-owned fintech major had, however, hired some 130 of ZestMoney's employees.
